evidence.label: An isomorphism of the free group factors

headline: Proves, with a Lean check, that the free group factors L(F₂) and L(F₃) are isomorphic, settling a decades-old problem.
scope: Group von Neumann algebras of free groups, including the interpolated free group factors L(F_r) for every r > 1 and r = ∞.
plain: A free group is made of words in some letters and their inverses, where a letter cancels next to its inverse. Each group gives an operator algebra. For decades it was open whether free groups on two and three letters give the same algebra. This paper constructs an isomorphism between them, so the answer is yes. Lean checks that all interpolated free group factors are isomorphic.
doesNot: This does not say the free groups themselves are isomorphic; F₂ and F₃ remain different groups.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.significanceWhy: The free group factor isomorphism problem is one of the best-known open problems in operator algebras.

explanation:
Write words in the letters a and b and their inverses A and B. Cancel any letter that sits next to its inverse, so aA disappears. What is left is the free group on two letters, F₂. It has 4 words of length one, 4 × 3 = 12 of length two and 36 of length three. With three letters, F₃ has 6, 30 and 150. These are different groups; no relabelling turns one into the other.

Each group gives an operator algebra, its group von Neumann algebra L(G). Every group element acts on square-summable sequences by shifting them. The algebra is the closure of these shifts. The free group factors arose in the foundational work of Murray and von Neumann[1]. Whether L(F_m) and L(F_n) are isomorphic for distinct m and n became a central problem in classifying finite factors[2]. Kadison is credited with raising the question.

Free probability gave tools but no answer. Dykema and Rădulescu built interpolated factors L(F_r) for every real r > 1. Their amplification formula says a resized copy of L(F_s) by factor t is L(F_r) with r = 1 + (s − 1)/t²[3]. They also gave a dichotomy: either all interpolated factors are isomorphic, or no two are[4]. So one isomorphism between two distinct ranks settles everything. The obstacle was to build one.

The paper proves that L(F_n) and L(F_(n+1)) are isomorphic for every n of at least 3[5]. It applies this at ranks 3 and 4, giving L(F₃) ≅ L(F₄) ≅ L(F₅). Now resize both ends by √2, so t² = 2. The formula gives 1 + (3 − 1)/2 = 2 and 1 + (5 − 1)/2 = 3. So L(F₂) ≅ L(F₃)[6]. With the dichotomy, all interpolated free group factors, including the infinite-rank one, are isomorphic[7]. The paper also deduces that their fundamental groups are all positive reals[8]. It answers negatively Voiculescu's question on free entropy dimension[9]. That question asked whether a numerical invariant of generators depends only on the algebra they generate.

The construction uses a flow, a continuous family of automorphisms built from a differential equation. Each step moves the n generators very little but makes a word in them approximate an extra generator. Repeating this absorbs the extra generator in the limit.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has a formal proof. It covers the isomorphism of interpolated free group factors for all parameters r, s > 1, including infinity. The fundamental-group statement is a further consequence and is not a separate Lean statement. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Landmark: it resolves the free group factor problem. Lean formally checks the isomorphism of all interpolated free group factors; no specialist review is published yet.

glossary.meaning: All words in n letters and their inverses, where the only rule is cancelling a letter next to its inverse.
The operator algebra generated by the shifts that group elements make on square-summable sequences.
A von Neumann algebra whose only central elements are multiples of the identity.
A one-to-one match between two algebras that keeps all the operations; here it also keeps the trace.
A factor L(F_r) defined for every real r > 1, agreeing with L(F_n) at whole numbers.
Resizing a factor by a factor t, by taking a corner or a larger matrix version.
The set of scales t at which the factor is isomorphic to its own resized copy.
A number attached to a set of generators, from Voiculescu's free probability theory.
